extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency policymakers, and researchers of notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical coding scheme and recommendations for assessing the sophistication and substantive quality of public comments submitted in notice-and-comment rulemakings; compares lay (citizen) versus sophisticated commenters across multiple proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the specific provision of the proposed rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment names or pins to the particular regulatory provision, section, or text of the proposed rule that it addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scorers should look for explicit reference to rule sections, paragraph citations, or quoted text indicating the comment is tied to discrete regulatory language rather than general policy preferences. (Related: 'pin to specific text' as a marker of sophistication.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite legal authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment references statutes, existing regulations, court decisions, or other legal authorities to support its claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes citation to relevant statutory provisions, regulatory cross-references, controlling or persuasive case law, or administratively relevant legal doctrines. Presence of legal authority demonstrates grounding in legal framework rather than mere opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite empirical evidence or data
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment provides empirical support such as studies, statistics, data, or other factual evidence to substantiate claims about effects or needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May include academic studies, agency or industry data, economic analyses, empirical reports, or concrete factual examples. Empirical/evidence-based content should be treated as substantive information rather than mere rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate a clear position
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment clearly states whether it supports, opposes, or suggests modification to the proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear normative stance (support/oppose/modify) helps agencies understand the commenter's recommendation; vague or ambiguous expressions of preference score lower on this dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with the agency's stated rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment responds to, critiques, or otherwise interacts with the agency's reasons, findings, or stated justification for the proposed rule instead of merely asserting preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit references to the agency's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking justification, counter-arguments, or efforts to connect commenter's evidence/position to the agency's stated goals. Engagement with agency rationale is a key marker of responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose alternative regulatory language or specific modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment offers concrete drafting suggestions, specific alternative language, or precise modifications to the proposed regulatory text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific, redactable language or detailed rule structure changes are higher-quality than abstract suggestions; such drafting aids agencies in implementing changes and demonstrates practical input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment acknowledges costs, burdens, or tradeoffs associated with the commenter's preferred position or the alternatives presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality comments weigh benefits against costs and show awareness of distributional impacts or feasibility concerns. Explicit recognition of tradeoffs signals reasoned policymaking rather than one-sided advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address likely opposing arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment anticipates and rebuts counterarguments or limitations to its own position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective comments strengthen persuasiveness by preemptively engaging probable objections, demonstrating critical assessment rather than simply asserting conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide experiential or lived-impact evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment supplies experiential evidence about real-world impacts (lived experience, downstream effects on vulnerable populations, implementation realities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cuéllar emphasizes that experiential evidence from lay commenters can reveal impacts sophisticated commenters miss; agencies and coders should treat such evidence as substantive input, not inferior anecdote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pin comments to specific text (rubric implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should link their points to exact passages of the proposal (overlaps with 'identify the specific provision').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit textual pinning increases comment usefulness; it helps agencies see precisely where and how the rule would change or operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies should provide plain-language summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory drafters/ agencies ought to supply accessible, plain-language explanations of proposed rules to make participation easier for lay commenters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural recommendation to improve comment quality and inclusiveness: plain-language synopses reduce comprehension barriers and enable substantive lay participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structured prompts on comment forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should include structured prompts on comment submission forms to elicit specific information from commenters (e.g., which provision, what evidence, suggested language).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured prompts can improve the responsiveness and sophistication of lay submissions by guiding commenters to hit useful markers (provision cited, empirical basis, tradeoffs, alternatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Require explicit agency responses to substantive lay comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should be required to explicitly address substantive lay comments in their decision documents rather than routinely discounting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cuéllar argues failure to credit lay comments is a procedural injustice; explicit responses improve democratic legitimacy and ensure meaningful consideration of experiential evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat experiential evidence as substantive in evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluators and agencies should consider lived-experience testimony and experiential impacts as legitimate substantive information when assessing comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shifts evaluative weight away from overvaluing formal legal/technical submissions and acknowledges that experiential reports can identify real-world consequences essential for rulemaking.
